titre: Göbekli Tepe, a Temple Predating Agriculture
accroche: More than 11,000 years ago, hunter-gatherers erect large limestone pillars at Göbekli Tepe, with no established agriculture at the site.
contenu_vulgarise:
In what is now southeastern Turkey, on a hill near Şanlıurfa, T-shaped limestone pillars, cut in quarries about a hundred meters from the hill, were set up in the Pre-Pottery Neolithic. When the German archaeologist Klaus Schmidt recognized the importance of the site in 1994, then began excavating it the following year, the question that forced itself was that of who had built it: the site shows, according to the French Wikipedia entry, “no certain trace” of agriculture.

## A Monumental Site of Hunter-Gatherers

The site was occupied from the 10th millennium BCE, well before writing and metals. Four circular enclosures have been excavated, and geophysical surveys indicate at least twenty large ones in all; nearly two hundred T-shaped pillars have been counted across all the structures. The reliefs show lions, bulls, wild boars, foxes, gazelles, donkeys, snakes, insects, and vultures. Some pillars bear human arms carved on their lower face and a loincloth: they are interpreted as the bodies of stylized human figures. The bones found in large numbers come from local game, deer, gazelles, pigs, and geese, which points to feasting. More than seven thousand grinding stones have also been recorded, which suggests the processing of cereals.

## What This Shifts

Klaus Schmidt, who directed the excavations until his death in 2014, defended the hypothesis of a ritual center where bands of hunter-gatherers gathered periodically to build and feast, and which may have contributed to the later development of urban civilization. In this reading, the monuments precede agricultural life instead of following it.

This reading is debated, and the picture of the site has evolved. The excavations have uncovered buildings of a domestic character, distinct from the ritual circular enclosures, and the idea of a deliberate burial, long accepted, has lost credit since Schmidt's death. A 2019 study of more than seven thousand grinding stones found at the site concludes, however, that there were seasonal peaks of activity rather than permanent residence: it sees in them the trace of large building projects and work feasts periodically bringing together labor, without the silos that would signal an established agricultural economy, and without settling whether the ground cereals, mainly einkorn and barley, were still wild or already in the process of domestication. This result, rather than contradicting Schmidt's hypothesis, gives it a more precise content: what took place here is less a village than a periodic gathering.

Inscribed on UNESCO's World Heritage List in 2018, Göbekli Tepe is presented as one of the earliest manifestations of monumental architecture built by humans.

repere.texte: Four circular enclosures excavated at Göbekli Tepe, at least twenty indicated by geophysical surveys, and nearly two hundred T-shaped pillars across all the structures; the site, occupied from the 10th millennium BCE, shows no certain trace of agriculture.

carte.punch: Monumental pillars, erected more than 11,000 years ago by hunter-gatherers.
carte.idee: At Göbekli Tepe, hunter-gatherers erect T-shaped limestone pillars as early as the 10th millennium BCE. Klaus Schmidt saw in it a ritual center that predates agriculture; a 2019 study on the grinding of cereals sees seasonal gatherings rather than a village.

quiz.question: Why does Göbekli Tepe upset the order usually attributed to the Neolithic revolution?
choix: Because metal tools far older than expected were found there, in the enclosures
Because hunter-gatherers erected large pillars there, with no certain trace of agriculture
Because the site proves that agriculture was born much earlier than was thought
Because it replaces Stonehenge as the oldest known monument in all of Europe
quiz.explication: The pillars of Göbekli Tepe were erected by hunter-gatherers, with no certain trace of agriculture at the site: Schmidt saw in it a ritual center predating agricultural life, a hypothesis that is debated but not refuted by recent research. No metal is mentioned there, and the site is in Turkey, not in Europe.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What do the reliefs carved on the T-shaped pillars of Göbekli Tepe show?
choix: Scenes of pitched battle between rival cities of the region
Agricultural calendars carved continuously along the whole height of the pillars
Inscriptions in cuneiform script describing in detail the rites practiced
Wild animals, lions, bulls, wild boars, snakes, vultures, and human arms on some pillars
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The reliefs show lions, bulls, wild boars, foxes, gazelles, donkeys, snakes, insects, and vultures, and some pillars bear carved human arms. No battle scene, no continuous agricultural calendar, and no cuneiform writing are mentioned.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What do the more than seven thousand grinding stones found at the site suggest, according to the 2019 study?
choix: A permanent residence comparable to an established farming village
The existence of storage silos for domesticated cereals
Seasonal peaks of activity, read as periodic building projects and work feasts
A cereal trade with regions located several hundred kilometers away
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The 2019 study on the grinding stones concludes there were seasonal peaks of activity rather than permanent residence, and notes the absence of silos that would signal an established agricultural economy. No long-distance trade is mentioned in the entry.
